cf.title: using index to speedup add not null constraints to a table

input.subject: using index to speedup add not null constraints to a table

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and a committer called the idea great in message #11. The open points are fixable design questions. maintenance-fit-1 asks which check guarantees the index is not rebuilt in the same alter table. maintenance-fit-2 asks for a cost bound when the index holds dead null entries. already-exists-1 stands only as a request to compare with `not valid` plus `validate constraint`.

brief.title: Use a btree index to validate new not-null constraints in alter table
brief.problem: Adding a not-null constraint to an existing table scans the whole heap to look for nulls, which is slow on large tables. The patch targets users who run alter table ... set not null or add constraint ... not null on big tables that already have a suitable index.
brief.proposed_design: In phase 3 of alter table, the patch collects all new not-null constraints and checks that each column is the leading column of a valid btree index. If no table scan or rewrite is needed, the table holds AccessExclusiveLock and no virtual generated column is involved, an index scan looks for one null under a fresh MVCC snapshot. Otherwise the normal table scan runs.
user_visible_surface: A DEBUG1 message: "all new not-null constraints on relation "%s" have been validated by using index scan".
Faster alter table ... alter column ... set not null and add constraint ... not null when a suitable index exists.
author_claims: On a table with 1 million deleted rows, adding not null took 1.873 ms with the patch against 648.312 ms on master.
In a later benchmark on 2 million rows, repeated runs took about 1.6 ms with an index against about 213 ms without one.
The v1 commit message says the patch can be slower than master when the index is bloated with dead null entries (1080 ms against 971 ms).
Under AccessExclusiveLock, a fresh MVCC snapshot sees the same rows a table scan would check, so the result is the same.
Using one multicolumn index for several non-leading columns was slower than a table scan, so only leading columns qualify.
brief.thread_state: Álvaro Herrera reviewed it, called it a great idea and asked for restructuring, then removed himself as committer in April 2026. Jian He posted v14 to v16 since then, and no reply to them is visible.
unclear: The material does not say whether the first slow run in bench.txt (about 480 ms in both cases) means index scan gains depend on a warm cache or hint bits.
Partitioned tables: v1 excluded them, and later versions do not say whether they are supported.
The proposal gives no bound on cost when the index holds many dead null entries and does not say whether bloat is checked first.
Nothing says whether indcheckxmin and invalid or partial indexes are all excluded, beyond the get_relation_info mirror.
No documentation change is shown, so users cannot tell when the fast path applies other than through the DEBUG1 message.
search_queries: index scan validate not null constraint
alter table set not null without table scan
not null constraint verify using index
alter table add constraint performance large table

objections.title: Correctness rests on an implicit list of phase 3 conditions
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds or changes an alter table subcommand so that an index is rebuilt or changed in the same command, and the fast-path checks are not updated. The index scan then runs on an index that does not match the final table. A not-null constraint is accepted while nulls exist, and users find out only when queries or pg_dump restores fail.
objections.argument: Message #1 and the v1 commit message show that subcommands which trigger index rebuilds, such as SET EXPRESSION, already broke this approach. v4 (message #4) listed "no new indexes" as a condition, but the v16 commit message lists only scan or rewrite, the lock level and virtual generated columns. The only tests are a TAP test that greps a DEBUG1 message (message #18), and none of them fails when a new subcommand changes these conditions.
objections.author_must_show: Which single check guarantees the chosen index is not rebuilt or changed in the same alter table, and what test fails if a future subcommand breaks that guarantee?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 shows that index rebuilds in the same command already broke the approach once. The v16 commit message no longer lists the v4 "no new indexes" condition, and nothing shown names the check that replaces it.

objections.title: No bound or opt-out when the index holds many dead nulls
objections.failure_scenario: An operator deletes or updates many rows that had nulls, and vacuum has not run. They then run set not null on a large table whose cache is cold. Each dead index entry needs a random heap fetch under AccessExclusiveLock, so the command can run longer than the sequential scan it replaced, and no setting turns the fast path off.
objections.argument: The v1 commit message reports that the patch is slower than master when null entries are bloated (1080 ms against 971 ms), and that test used a warm table with only a million rows. In bench.txt the first run took about 480 ms with and without the index, so the gains shown come from repeated runs on a warm cache. The patch picks the index path whenever an index exists and does not look at cost or bloat first.
objections.author_must_show: How slow is the index path on a cold cache when the index holds many dead null entries, and why is choosing it with no cost check safe enough?

critic.reasoning: The v1 commit message reports the slowdown with dead null entries, and no later version gives a bound or a cost check. In bench.txt the indexed table has dead null entries, and its first run is no faster than the table scan.

objections.title: Overlap with the existing not valid plus validate constraint path
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA with a large table runs `alter table ... add constraint ... not null` and expects the index fast path. If the index is bloated, the cache is cold, or a second clause forces a scan, the full scan runs under AccessExclusiveLock. The existing path would have avoided that lock: add a not valid constraint, then run validate constraint, which takes a weaker lock.
objections.argument: Postgres already supports adding a not-null constraint as `not valid` and validating it later with `validate constraint` under ShareUpdateExclusiveLock, so writes continue during the scan. Older releases had the same option through a validated `check (col is not null)` constraint, which lets `set not null` skip the scan. The proposal makes the one-step command faster but does not compare itself with these paths. In bench.txt the first run is about the same with and without the index (about 480 ms), so the gain may depend on a warm cache.
objections.author_must_show: For which users is `not valid` plus `validate constraint` not enough, and does the index path still help on a cold cache?

critic.reasoning: `not valid` plus `validate constraint` avoids the long AccessExclusiveLock, and the thread does not compare the patch with it. The failure scenario describes current behaviour, so the objection stands only as a request for that comparison.

refuted.title: No field evidence that the indexed case is common or unsolved
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA has a large table and the target column is not the leading column of a valid btree index. The DBA runs set not null, still gets a full scan under AccessExclusiveLock, and keeps using check (col is not null) not valid plus validate. The new code path then helps few of the users who have this problem.
refuted.argument: Users who want a fast set not null must add the check constraint themselves, then validate it, and Postgres then skips the scan. The fast path applies only when the column leads a btree index and no scan or rewrite is pending (message #4, message #13). The thread has no user report and no -general or -bugs reference. Its demand rests on an older design suggestion and a reviewer calling it a great idea (message #1, message #11), and it does not say how often production tables meet the index condition.
refuted.author_must_show: Which user reports show large tables that need set not null, already have a leading-column btree index, and cannot use the check-constraint workaround?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which asks the same question about the existing workaround. The rest is weak: the scenario describes current behaviour, a committer called the idea great in message #11, and the patch adds no cost for other users.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: see objection maintenance-fit-2: No bound or opt-out when the index holds many dead nulls

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The fast path in tablecmds.c depends on a list of phase 3 conditions that later alter table subcommands must keep true.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The index scan runs under AccessExclusiveLock and was slower than the table scan when the index held dead null entries.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: `not valid` plus `validate constraint` already avoids the long scan under AccessExclusiveLock.

questions: Which single check guarantees that the chosen index is not rebuilt or changed in the same alter table, and which test fails if a future subcommand breaks it?
How slow is the index scan on a cold cache when the index holds many dead null entries, compared with the table scan?
Why is it safe to choose the index scan with no cost or bloat check, given the 1080 ms against 971 ms result in the v1 commit message?
For which users is `not valid` plus `validate constraint` not enough, so that the one-step fast path is needed?
Does v16 use the index scan for partitioned tables, and does it exclude partial, invalid and expression indexes?

committability.owner_note: Needs a committer who knows alter table phase 3 and not-null constraints. Álvaro Herrera reviewed it in the thread but removed himself as committer in April 2026.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the claim that the index scan never accepts a not-null constraint while a null exists, for every future alter table subcommand combination.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted sixteen versions over almost two years and kept rebasing after the committer left, so follow-up looks likely.

priority.reason: The patch helps only when the column leads a valid btree index and no scan or rewrite is pending. v16 touches only tablecmds.c and adds no user-visible surface, but it has had no committer since April 2026 and no visible reply to v14 to v16.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review cannot confirm which indexes the patch excludes or that the phase 3 conditions cover every subcommand that rebuilds an index. The visibility argument in the v16 commit message was also not checked against the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Change a constraint's index - ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX ...
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Alvaro Herrera, Laurenz Albe
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX to replace the index behind an EXCLUDE, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY or FOREIGN KEY constraint with a similar index. The main use case is swapping a primary key index for one with INCLUDE columns, or back.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane wanted the feature rejected because a primary key with a swapped index is no longer an accurate primary key, and information_schema cannot describe it. Alvaro Herrera and Laurenz Albe agreed that primary keys with INCLUDE columns would first need PRIMARY KEY syntax, so that pg_dump works. That leaves this command a narrow use case. The author did not answer the review, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.

fast constraint validation index

precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
TBH I think if we really wanted the feature of primary keys with
included columns, we'd have to add it to the PRIMARY KEY syntax rather
than having an ad-hoc ALTER TABLE ALTER CONSTRAINT USING INDEX command
to replace the index underneath.

precedents_retrieved.title: avoid bitmapOR-ing indexes for scan conditions implied by partition constraint
precedents_retrieved.authors: Justin Pryzby (justinpryzby), Soumyadeep Chakraborty (soumyadeep2007), Soumyadeep Chakraborty (soumyadeepc)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner skip bitmap index scans for arms of an OR clause that the partition constraint refutes, so each partition scans only the useful arms. The change lives in generate_bitmap_or_paths() in indxpath.c and targets queries with long OR lists over many partitions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to fixing this in indxpath.c. The fix helps only bitmap scans, may repeat the same proof, cannot be turned off, leaves row estimates unchanged, and may break the loop that requires each OR arm to match an index. He proposed removing proven quals from baserestrictinfo instead, but measured about 2.5% slowdown on pgbench -S and left the direction open. The entry then sat in Waiting on Author for weeks, and Masahiko Sawada returned it with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve amcheck to check UNIQUE constraint in btree index
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Geoghegan, Mark Dilger, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend contrib/amcheck's bt_index_check and bt_index_parent_check so that, for btree indexes with a UNIQUE constraint, they detect duplicate keys whose heap tuples are visible, including duplicates spanning adjacent leaf pages, and report the index and heap TIDs involved. Later versions added an optional argument to enable the uniqueness check and a regression test variant for 32-bit systems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers asked for further changes: Peter Geoghegan objected to reporting violations as WARNINGs, to the message saying an index only might be corrupt (calling it an unacceptable false positive), to the handling of cross-page duplicates, and to tests that update pg_index, and suggested opclass-based fault injection and sharing the heapallindexed snapshot. Mark Dilger's review of v4 asked for documentation updates, pg_amcheck integration with TAP tests, and a different test approach. No updated patch followed for several weeks, and David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it needed more work and had not been updated.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prevent ALTER TABLE DROP NOT NULL on child tables if parent column has it
precedents_retrieved.summary: Prevent ALTER TABLE ... DROP NOT NULL on a child table when the same column in a parent table is marked NOT NULL, so that the constraint can only be dropped from the parent. precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

roaster_notes.note: The only listed precedent, [P6], is about making an existing index unique with NOT VALID. It stalled because its author ran out of time, a reason that does not apply here. Message #1 says this design follows an earlier list suggestion to pull one null from an index, which warned it 'needs careful thought because of visibility issues'. The v16 commit message answers that warning with the AccessExclusiveLock and fresh-snapshot argument, and message #21 adds the indcheckxmin check, so the prior-attempts angle finds no rejection reason left open.

The patch adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog column or psql change, and pg_dump output is unchanged. The fast path only replaces the heap scan inside existing alter table commands under the same lock, so existing scripts and dumps get the same result. Safety and the bloated-index cost belong to other angles.

The proposal adds no persistent or cross-node state: v16 touches only tablecmds.c and changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire message or exported API. The standby replays the same catalog change, and the commit message explains why the MVCC invariant holds under AccessExclusiveLock. Without the code, this angle cannot check that the indcheckxmin and invalid-index exclusions match the commit message.

The proposal adds no privilege, role or setting, and the fast path runs only inside alter table, which already requires table ownership and takes AccessExclusiveLock. A btree null search needs no user-defined comparison code, and the only new output is a DEBUG1 message naming the relation. Whether expression and partial indexes are excluded is a correctness question for other angles, and it cannot be checked without the code.

The cost falls only on alter table with not-null validation, and nothing changes for other paths. The patch has had no committer since April 2026, which matters for committability but not for the verdict.
One objection only. The existing alternative works with modest extra steps, so this is a question of convenience and not of capability.

The problem is real, the change adds no syntax or GUC, and the cost falls mostly on users who hit the fast path. A committer called it a great idea in message #11, so this is a request for demand evidence, not a rejection.
